title: SSRF filter bypass (regex not applied post-resolution)
summary:
### Summary
The internal-IP SSRF filter can be bypassed in specific non-default configuration. 

When an operator disables non-global-IP block (`HTTP_REQUEST_BLOCK_NON_GLOBAL_IPS=false`) and instead relies on `HTTP_REQUEST_BLOCK_REGEX` to keep the server's outbound HTTP client (icon fetching, etc.) away from internal ranges, the regex is **never applied to resolved IP addresses**. An unauthenticated attacker can therefore reach a regex-blocked internal IP by supplying a hostname that resolves to that IP but does not textually match the regex,via unauthenticated `/icons/<host>/icon.png` endpoint.

Default installs are **not** affected.

This is a residual gap in the same fixes implemented for CVE-2026-47160 / GHSA-72vh-x5jq-m82g (fixed in 1.36.0). That fix closed decimal/hex/octal IP-format bypass which affected the _default_ config. This report is a distinct gap, the regex is not applied post-resolution, that affects _regex-reliance_ config and is present in 1.36.0 and earlier. It is fixed in 1.37.0.

### Details
The pre-connect and post-resolution filters are asymmetric.

`should_block_host()` (src/http_client.rs:135) applies **both** checks to an IP
host - `should_block_ip()` and `should_block_address_regex()`. But
`post_resolve()` (src/http_client.rs:273) applies **only** `should_block_ip()`:

    // src/http_client.rs:273 @ tag 1.36.0
    fn post_resolve(name: &str, ip: IpAddr) -> Result<(), CustomHttpClientError> {
        if should_block_ip(ip) {
            Err(CustomHttpClientError::NonGlobalIp { domain: Some(name.to_string()), ip })
        } else {
            Ok(())
        }
    }

`should_block_ip()` (src/http_client.rs:61) short-circuits to `false` for every
IP when the non-global-IP block is disabled:

    fn should_block_ip(ip: IpAddr) -> bool {
        if !CONFIG.http_request_block_non_global_ips() {   // default: true
            return false;
        }
        !is_global(ip)
    }

So with `http_request_block_non_global_ips=false`, the regex
(`http_request_block_regex`, src/config.rs:703) is the *only* protection for
internal ranges - yet `resolve_domain()` (src/http_client.rs:241) only runs it
against the domain string in `pre_resolve()` (src/http_client.rs:257), never
against the resolved IP in `post_resolve()`.

For a URL whose host is a domain name, the flow is:

  1. pre_resolve() -> should_block_host(Host::Domain(name)) -> regex tested
     against the **domain string** only. A hostname that does not textually
     contain the target IP does not match an IP-pattern regex -> pass.
  2. DNS resolves the name to an internal IP.
  3. post_resolve(name, ip) -> should_block_ip(ip) -> false (flag disabled)
     -> regex is never applied to the IP -> allowed.

The request then proceeds to the internal IP. In contrast, the same IP supplied
as a literal is caught, because should_block_host() (used for IP-literal hosts
at src/api/icons.rs:123) does apply the regex.

Entry point: `icon_internal` (src/api/icons.rs:111, `#[get("/<host>/icon.png")]`)
is unauthenticated and drives this outbound fetch through the shared reqwest
client + custom DNS resolver. Other outbound requests that use the shared
resolver (push relay, HIBP, Duo, version check) were also affected, but their
destinations are fixed or administrator-configured, so the attacker-reachable
entry point is the unauthenticated icon endpoint.

Affected source (line numbers per tag 1.36.0, src/http_client.rs unless noted):
  - post_resolve            :273   (root cause - only should_block_ip)
  - should_block_ip         :61    (flag short-circuit)
  - should_block_address_regex :69
  - should_block_host       :135   (correct: both checks)
  - resolve_domain          :241   (pre_resolve + per-IP post_resolve)
  - pre_resolve             :257   (regex on domain string only)
  - icon_internal route     :111   (src/api/icons.rs, unauthenticated)
